claim: Over thirty classes of functionally and morphologically distinct retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exist in mammals.
source: Over thirty classes of functionally and morphologically distinct retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exist in mammals, each responsible for conveying different features of the visual world and each with unique projections to retinorecipient nuclei within the brain (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016

claim: Each class of RGC is responsible for conveying different features of the visual world.
source: Over thirty classes of functionally and morphologically distinct retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exist in mammals, each responsible for conveying different features of the visual world and each with unique projections to retinorecipient nuclei within the brain (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016

claim: Each class of RGC has unique projections to retinorecipient nuclei within the brain.
source: Over thirty classes of functionally and morphologically distinct retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exist in mammals, each responsible for conveying different features of the visual world and each with unique projections to retinorecipient nuclei within the brain (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanes and Masland, 2015; Martersteck et al., 2017; Baden et al., 2016

claim: RGCs innervate over 40 retinorecipient brain regions.
source: As a group, RGCs innervate over 40 retinorecipient brain regions (Morin and Studholme, 2014; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morin and Studholme, 2014; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017

claim: Only a subset of RGCs (~50%) innervate relay cells in the visual thalamus (i.e. the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus [dLGN]).
source: However, only a subset of RGCs (~50%) innervate relay cells in the visual thalamus (i.e. the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus [dLGN]) and provide the principal pathway for image-forming visual information to reach the cerebral cortex (Dhande et al., 2015; Seabrook et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dhande et al., 2015; Seabrook et al., 2017

claim: RGCs that innervate dLGN provide the principal pathway for image-forming visual information to reach the cerebral cortex.
source: However, only a subset of RGCs (~50%) innervate relay cells in the visual thalamus (i.e. the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus [dLGN]) and provide the principal pathway for image-forming visual information to reach the cerebral cortex (Dhande et al., 2015; Seabrook et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dhande et al., 2015; Seabrook et al., 2017

claim: RGC inputs are segregated into distinct class-specific sublamina within visual thalamus.
source: The recent development of transgenic tools to label these classes of RGCs has revealed that their inputs are segregated into distinct class-specific sublamina within visual thalamus (Huberman et al., 2008; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017; Huberman et al., 2009; Kay et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2008, 2010; Hong and Chen, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huberman et al., 2008; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017; Huberman et al., 2009; Kay et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2008, 2010; Hong and Chen, 2011

claim: Different features of the visual field are transmitted through the subcortical visual system in parallel, unmixed anatomical channels.
source: supporting the longstanding belief that different features of the visual field are transmitted through the subcortical visual system in parallel, unmixed anatomical channels (Dhande et al., 2015; Cruz-Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dhande et al., 2015; Cruz-Martín et al., 2014

claim: VGluT2+ retinal terminals undergo significant enlargement in dLGN at eye-opening (P12-P14).
source: However, by eye-opening (P12-P14), terminals in dLGN underwent significant enlargement compared to those in vLGN and other (Hammer et al., 2014) retinorecipient nuclei (Figure 1B–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Hammer et al., 2014

claim: VGluT2+ retinal terminals in vLGN do not undergo significant enlargement at eye-opening.
source: However, by eye-opening (P12-P14), terminals in dLGN underwent significant enlargement compared to those in vLGN and other (Hammer et al., 2014) retinorecipient nuclei (Figure 1B–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Hammer et al., 2014

claim: Retinal terminals from Mnx1-GFP labeled ON-OFF direction-selective RGCs are larger in dLGN than in SC (0.83 ± 0.1 µm2 in dLGN vs 0.36 ± 0.01 µm in SC, p<0.01).
source: Despite originating from branches of individual retinal axons, those terminals present in dLGN were dramatically larger than those in SC (0.83 ± 0.1 µm2 in dLGN vs 0.36 ± 0.01 µm in SC, p<0.01 by t-test, n = 3, Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1I,J with statistical analysis

claim: Target-derived cues are generated in dLGN around the time of eye-opening to pattern the transformation of retinal terminals.
source: These data suggest that target-derived cues are generated in dLGN around the time of eye-opening to pattern the transformation of retinal terminals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that terminals from the same RGC class differ in size between dLGN and SC

claim: Both simple and complex RG synapses are present shortly after eye-opening (P14).
source: While SBFSEM ultrastructural analysis revealed the presence of both simple and complex RG synapses shortly after eye-opening (P14) we were only able to identify simple-like RG synapses prior to eye-opening (at P8) (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 1K

claim: Only simple-like RG synapses are present prior to eye-opening (at P8).
source: While SBFSEM ultrastructural analysis revealed the presence of both simple and complex RG synapses shortly after eye-opening (P14) we were only able to identify simple-like RG synapses prior to eye-opening (at P8) (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 1K

claim: Clusters of retinal terminals originating from distinct RGCs are present as early as P10 and P14.
source: brainbow AAV-labeling failed to detect clusters of retinal terminals at P8 (Figure 1M), but clearly revealed clusters of retinal terminals originating from distinct RGCs as early as P10 and P14 (Figure 1N,O).
evidence: Supported by brainbow AAV labeling data shown in Figure 1M-O

claim: Clusters of retinal terminals are not detected at P8 by brainbow AAV-labeling.
source: brainbow AAV-labeling failed to detect clusters of retinal terminals at P8 (Figure 1M), but clearly revealed clusters of retinal terminals originating from distinct RGCs as early as P10 and P14 (Figure 1N,O).
evidence: Supported by brainbow AAV labeling data shown in Figure 1M

claim: Lrrtm1 mRNA is significantly enriched in dLGN compared to vLGN at eye-opening.
source: Two genes with well-established roles in inducing excitatory synapses fit those criteria: Lrrtm1 and neuritin 1 (Nrn1) (Figure 2C–E) (Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2C-E and citations to Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005

claim: Nrn1 mRNA is significantly enriched in dLGN compared to vLGN at eye-opening.
source: Two genes with well-established roles in inducing excitatory synapses fit those criteria: Lrrtm1 and neuritin 1 (Nrn1) (Figure 2C–E) (Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2C-E and citations to Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005

claim: Lrrtm1 has a well-established role in inducing excitatory synapses.
source: Two genes with well-established roles in inducing excitatory synapses fit those criteria: Lrrtm1 and neuritin 1 (Nrn1) (Figure 2C–E) (Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Linhoff et al., 2009

claim: Nrn1 has a well-established role in inducing excitatory synapses.
source: Two genes with well-established roles in inducing excitatory synapses fit those criteria: Lrrtm1 and neuritin 1 (Nrn1) (Figure 2C–E) (Linhoff et al., 2009; Javaherian and Cline, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Javaherian and Cline, 2005

claim: Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs are either absent or only weakly expressed in SC and SCN.
source: In addition to their low expression level in vLGN, it is important to point out that Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs were either absent or only weakly expressed in other retinorecipient nuclei, such as the SC and suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Lrrtm1 is not generated by RGCs.
source: Lrrtm1 was not generated by RGCs (although it was expressed in the INL) or by many cells in primary visual cortex (vCTX) (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Lrrtm1 is expressed in the INL of the retina.
source: Lrrtm1 was not generated by RGCs (although it was expressed in the INL) or by many cells in primary visual cortex (vCTX) (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Lrrtm1 is not expressed by many cells in primary visual cortex (vCTX).
source: Lrrtm1 was not generated by RGCs (although it was expressed in the INL) or by many cells in primary visual cortex (vCTX) (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Nrn1 is robustly expressed by RGCs.
source: whereas Nrn1 was robustly expressed by both RGCs and by cells in vCTX (Figure 3E,F) (see also Fujino et al., 2008; Nedivi et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E,F and citations to Fujino et al., 2008; Nedivi et al., 1998

claim: Nrn1 is robustly expressed by cells in vCTX.
source: whereas Nrn1 was robustly expressed by both RGCs and by cells in vCTX (Figure 3E,F) (see also Fujino et al., 2008; Nedivi et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 3E,F and citations to Fujino et al., 2008; Nedivi et al., 1998

claim: 93% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Lrrtm1.
source: First, we demonstrated that both Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs are generated by neurons and not glia since they were co-expressed by Syt1-expressing neurons (93% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Lrrtm1; 98% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Nrn1; Figure 4A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H)
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: 98% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Nrn1.
source: First, we demonstrated that both Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs are generated by neurons and not glia since they were co-expressed by Syt1-expressing neurons (93% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Lrrtm1; 98% of Syt1+ neurons co-expressed Nrn1; Figure 4A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H)
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs are not expressed by IBA1-expressing microglia.
source: but not by IBA1-expressing microglia or GFP-labeled astrocytes in Aldh1l1-GFP mice (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: Supported by ISH and IHC data shown in Figure 4C-F

claim: Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 mRNAs are not expressed by GFP-labeled astrocytes in Aldh1l1-GFP mice.
source: but not by IBA1-expressing microglia or GFP-labeled astrocytes in Aldh1l1-GFP mice (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: Supported by ISH and IHC data shown in Figure 4C-F

claim: 100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1.
source: Results revealed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells (100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1; 0% and 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1, respectively; Figure 4G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: 100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Nrn1.
source: Results revealed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells (100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1; 0% and 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1, respectively; Figure 4G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: 0% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1.
source: Results revealed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells (100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1; 0% and 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1, respectively; Figure 4G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Nrn1.
source: Results revealed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells (100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1; 0% and 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1, respectively; Figure 4G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells.
source: Results revealed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1 are exclusively produced by dLGN relay cells (100% of Crh-Cre::tdt+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1; 0% and 2% of Gad1+ cells co-expressed Lrrtm1 and Nrn1, respectively; Figure 4G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: There is a significant decrease in the number of large VGluT2+ puncta in dLGN of Lrrtm1−/− mice at and after eye-opening.
source: These studies revealed a significant decrease in the number of large VGluT2+ and CTB+ puncta in dLGN of Lrrtm1−/− mice at and after eye-opening (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,E)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,E

claim: There is a significant decrease in the number of large CTB+ puncta in dLGN of Lrrtm1−/− mice at and after eye-opening.
source: These studies revealed a significant decrease in the number of large VGluT2+ and CTB+ puncta in dLGN of Lrrtm1−/− mice at and after eye-opening (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,E)
evidence: Supported by anterograde labeling data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,E

claim: Retinal terminals in neonatal dLGN (i.e. before eye-opening) are not affected by the loss of LRRTM1.
source: Retinal terminals in neonatal dLGN (i.e. before eye-opening) or in vLGN were not affected by the loss of LRRTM1 (Figure 5A–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: Retinal terminals in vLGN are not affected by the loss of LRRTM1.
source: Retinal terminals in neonatal dLGN (i.e. before eye-opening) or in vLGN were not affected by the loss of LRRTM1 (Figure 5A–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: Non-retinal inputs examined in dLGN are not affected in Lrrtm1−/− mutant mice.
source: None of the non-retinal inputs examined appeared affected in Lrrtm1−/− mutant mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G-I

claim: Nrn1−/− mutants do not show developmental deficits in the density, size or distribution of retinal terminal in dLGN.
source: Similar analysis in Nrn1−/− mutants failed to identify developmental deficits in the density, size or distribution of retinal terminal in dLGN (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: 90% of RG synapses were classified as complex in control dLGN.
source: While the majority (90%) of RG synapses were classified as complex in controls, only 37% of retinal terminals fell into this category in Lrrtm1−/− mutant dLGN (Figure 6A–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Only 37% of retinal terminals were classified as complex in Lrrtm1−/− mutant dLGN.
source: While the majority (90%) of RG synapses were classified as complex in controls, only 37% of retinal terminals fell into this category in Lrrtm1−/− mutant dLGN (Figure 6A–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The majority of retinal terminal clusters in Lrrtm1−/− mutants (82.6%) contained less than four distinct inputs.
source: The majority of retinal terminal clusters in mutants (82.6%) contained less than four distinct inputs (identified by their unique colors).
evidence: Supported by brainbow AAV labeling analysis

claim: The majority (80%) of clusters in controls contained more than four distinct retinal terminals.
source: In contrast, the majority (80%) of clusters in controls contained more than four distinct retinal terminals.
evidence: Supported by brainbow AAV labeling analysis

claim: In control dLGN about 86% of complex RG synapses contained between 4–14 retinal terminals.
source: In control dLGN about 86% of complex RG synapses contained between 4–14 retinal terminals, whereas the majority of complex RG synapses in Lrrtm1−/− mutants contained only 2 or 3 inputs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The majority of complex RG synapses in Lrrtm1−/− mutants contained only 2 or 3 inputs.
source: In control dLGN about 86% of complex RG synapses contained between 4–14 retinal terminals, whereas the majority of complex RG synapses in Lrrtm1−/− mutants contained only 2 or 3 inputs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6C

claim: There is no significant loss of RGC axons in the optic nerves of Lrrtm1−/− mice.
source: While the reduced number of complex RG synapses (and retinal inputs at the few persisting complex RG synapses) might be caused by fewer retinal axons in mutants, we failed to observe a significant loss of RGC axons in the optic nerves of Lrrtm1−/− mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by optic nerve analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: There is an increase in individual retinal terminal size in both simple and complex RG synapses in Lrrtm1−/− mice.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed an increase in individual retinal terminal size in both simple and complex RG synapses in Lrrtm1−/− mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The increase in terminal size in Lrrtm1−/− mutant dLGN is accompanied by a significant increase in active zone number compared to control RG synapses.
source: This increase in terminal size in Lrrtm1−/− mutant dLGN was accompanied by a significant increase in active zone number compared to control RG synapses (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6E

claim: When active zone number is normalized to terminal size there is no difference in the density of active zones in control and mutant RG synapses.
source: However, when we normalized active zone number to terminal size there was no difference in the density of active zones in control and mutant RG synapses (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Atoh7−/− mice are unable to perform the two-alternative forced swim visual task.
source: Atoh7−/− mice were unable to perform this task, demonstrating the importance of vision in this assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Lrrtm1−/− mutants and controls display equal abilities to distinguish vertical gratings from a gray screen or horizontal gratings at the end of training.
source: Lrrtm1−/− mutants and controls displayed equal abilities to distinguish the vertical gratings (i.e. the positive visual cue) from a gray screen or horizontal gratings at the end of training, although the initial learning phase of Lrrtm1−/− mice was modestly impaired (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: The initial learning phase of Lrrtm1−/− mice is modestly impaired.
source: Lrrtm1−/− mutants and controls displayed equal abilities to distinguish the vertical gratings (i.e. the positive visual cue) from a gray screen or horizontal gratings at the end of training, although the initial learning phase of Lrrtm1−/− mice was modestly impaired (Figure 7B,C)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: Visual acuity is similar between Lrrtm1−/− mutants and controls, both falling below the 70% correct criteria at spatial frequencies above 0.57 cpd.
source: Results indicate that acuity was similar between mutants and controls, both falling below the 70% correct criteria at spatial frequencies above 0.57 cpd (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Lrrtm1−/− mutants do not show significant differences in contrast sensitivity compared to wild type mice.
source: Next, we altered the contrast of the vertical grating bars rather than the spatial frequency or orientation. Similarly, Lrrtm1−/− mutants failed to show significant differences compared to wild type mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Lrrtm1−/− mutants do not exhibit deficits in visual acuity, simple pattern recognition or contrast sensitivity.
source: Taken together these results suggest Lrrtm1−/− mutants do not exhibit deficits in visual acuity, simple pattern recognition or contrast sensitivity.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing no significant differences in simple visual tasks

claim: Lrrtm1−/− mutants perform significantly worse than controls in differentiating vertical and horizontal gratings while increasing the spatial frequency.
source: For example, we challenged mice to differentiate vertical and horizontal gratings while increasing the spatial frequency. In this more complex task, we found Lrrtm1−/− mutants performed significantly worse than controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: While control mice are able to discriminate vertical and horizontal bars at a spatial frequency of 0.32 cpd, Lrrtm1−/− mice performance drops significantly under the 70% threshold during these more complex tasks.
source: Interestingly, while control mice were able to discriminate vertical and horizontal bars at a spatial frequency of 0.32 cpd, Lrrtm1−/− mice performance dropped significantly under the 70% threshold during these more complex tasks (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F

claim: At lower contrast (i.e. 25% and 10%) Lrrtm1−/− mutant mice lack the sensitivity to discriminate vertical and horizontal grating patterns.
source: Similarly, at lower contrast (i.e. 25% and 10%) mutant mice lacked the sensitivity to discriminate vertical and horizontal grating patterns (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Nrn1−/− mutants show no deficit in their performance in either the simple or complex visual tasks.
source: As another set of controls, we repeated these behavioral tasks with Nrn1−/− mutants and found no deficit in their performance in either the simple or complex visual tasks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-J

claim: Mice lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapses exhibit abnormalities in performing more complex visual tasks.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that mice lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapses exhibit abnormalities in performing more complex visual tasks.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing deficits in complex but not simple visual tasks

claim: Retinal terminals in dLGN are prototypic 'driver' inputs which are large compared to adjacent non-retinal inputs.
source: Retinal terminals in dLGN are prototypic 'driver' inputs which are large (compared to adjacent non-retinal inputs) and capable of generating strong excitatory postsynaptic responses in thalamic relay cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammer et al., 2014

claim: Retinal terminals in dLGN are capable of generating strong excitatory postsynaptic responses in thalamic relay cells.
source: Retinal terminals in dLGN are prototypic 'driver' inputs which are large (compared to adjacent non-retinal inputs) and capable of generating strong excitatory postsynaptic responses in thalamic relay cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammer et al., 2014

claim: It was thought that only a few (1-5) RGCs innervate each relay cell.
source: Until recently, it was thought that the level of convergence of retinal inputs onto these relay cells was exceptionally low with only a few (1-5) RGCs innervating each relay cell (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005; Sincich et al., 2007; Hamos et al., 1987; Cleland and Lee, 1985; Cleland et al., 1971; Mastronarde, 1992; Usrey et al., 1999; Yeh et al., 2009; Weyand, 2016; Rathbun et al., 2016, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Regehr, 2000; Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005; Sincich et al., 2007; Hamos et al., 1987; Cleland and Lee, 1985; Cleland et al., 1971; Mastronarde, 1992; Usrey et al., 1999; Yeh et al., 2009; Weyand, 2016; Rathbun et al., 2016, 2010

claim: Recent anatomical studies in mice have revealed a level of retinal convergence onto relay cells that is more than an order of magnitude higher than previously described.
source: Recently, however, a series of anatomical studies in mice have challenged the concept of feature-specific, parallel visual channels by revealing a level of retinal convergence onto relay cells that is more than an order of magnitude higher than previously described (Hammer et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2016; Rompani et al., 2017; Howarth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammer et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2016; Rompani et al., 2017; Howarth et al., 2014

claim: Some relay cells receive input from functionally distinct classes of RGCs.
source: Not only is there a high level of retinogeniculate (RG) convergence in mice, but some relay cells receive input from functionally distinct classes of RGCs (Rompani et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rompani et al., 2017

claim: Complex RG synapses contain numerous retinal axons whose terminals aggregate on shared regions of relay cell dendrites.
source: Part of this newly appreciated retinal convergence stems from a set of unique RG synapses (termed complex RG synapses) that contain numerous retinal axons whose terminals aggregate on shared regions of relay cell dendrites (Morgan et al., 2016; Hammer et al., 2015; Lund and Cunningham, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morgan et al., 2016; Hammer et al., 2015; Lund and Cunningham, 1972

claim: Complex RG synapses have been reported in both rodents and higher mammals.
source: Complex RG synapses have been reported in both rodents and higher mammals (Lund and Cunningham, 1972; Jones and Powell, 1969; So et al., 1985; Campbell and Frost, 1987; Guillery and Scott, 1971; Wilson et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lund and Cunningham, 1972; Jones and Powell, 1969; So et al., 1985; Campbell and Frost, 1987; Guillery and Scott, 1971; Wilson et al., 1984

claim: Complex RG synapses are absent from other retinorecipient regions of brain.
source: Similar to the more classical simple RG synapses (which contain a single retinal terminal on a given portion of a relay cell dendrite), these complex RG synapses are absent from other retinorecipient regions of brain (Hammer et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammer et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Branches of dLGN-projecting RGCs also innervate other retinorecipient nuclei.
source: Since branches of dLGN-projecting RGCs also innervate other retinorecipient nuclei (Dhande et al., 2015), we interpret this to suggest that target-derived signals must be generated in dLGN to pattern the unique transformation of retinal axons into simple and complex RG synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dhande et al., 2015

claim: Target-derived signals must be generated in dLGN to pattern the unique transformation of retinal axons into simple and complex RG synapses.
source: Since branches of dLGN-projecting RGCs also innervate other retinorecipient nuclei (Dhande et al., 2015), we interpret this to suggest that target-derived signals must be generated in dLGN to pattern the unique transformation of retinal axons into simple and complex RG synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that complex RG synapses are unique to dLGN despite RGCs projecting to multiple targets

claim: LRRTM1 is a known inducer of excitatory synaptogenesis.
source: Using next generation sequencing, we discovered that relay cells in dLGN (but not principal neurons in other retinorecipient nuclei) express Leucine Rich Repeat Transmembrane Neuronal 1 (LRRTM1), a known inducer of excitatory synaptogenesis (Linhoff et al., 2009; de Wit et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Linhoff et al., 2009; de Wit et al., 2009

claim: Genetic deletion of LRRTM1 led to a loss of complex RG synapses.
source: Genetic deletion of LRRTM1 led to a loss of complex RG synapses and thus reduced retinal convergence in visual thalamus.
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM and brainbow AAV data

claim: Genetic deletion of LRRTM1 led to reduced retinal convergence in visual thalamus.
source: Genetic deletion of LRRTM1 led to a loss of complex RG synapses and thus reduced retinal convergence in visual thalamus.
evidence: Supported by SBFSEM and brainbow AAV data

claim: Mutants lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapse exhibit normal visual acuity.
source: While mutants lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapse exhibit normal visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, they display impaired performance in a set of more complex visual tasks that require processing multiple distinct elements of the visual field.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data

claim: Mutants lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapse exhibit normal contrast sensitivity.
source: While mutants lacking LRRTM1 and complex RG synapse exhibit normal visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, they display impaired performance in a set of more complex visual tasks that require processing multiple distinct elements of the visual field.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data

claim: LRRTMs are transmembrane proteins that act as transsynaptic signals to trigger excitatory synaptogenesis.
source: LRRTMs are transmembrane proteins that act as transsynaptic signals to trigger excitatory synaptogenesis (Linhoff et al., 2009; de Wit et al., 2009; de Wit and Ghosh, 2014; Um et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Linhoff et al., 2009; de Wit et al., 2009; de Wit and Ghosh, 2014; Um et al., 2016

claim: When present in the postsynaptic membrane, LRRTM1 binds to the extracellular domain of neurexins to induce presynaptic differentiation in contacting axons.
source: When present in the postsynaptic membrane, LRRTM1 binds to the extracellular domain of neurexins to induce presynaptic differentiation in contacting axons (Linhoff et al., 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Linhoff et al., 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2010

claim: LRRTM1 is specifically expressed by relay cells in visual thalamus.
source: In visual thalamus, LRRTM1 is specifically expressed by relay cells (and not other cells) and its transsynaptic partners, neurexins, are generated by RGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sajgo et al., 2017; Shigeoka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to Sajgo et al., 2017; Shigeoka et al., 2016

claim: Neurexins are generated by RGCs.
source: In visual thalamus, LRRTM1 is specifically expressed by relay cells (and not other cells) and its transsynaptic partners, neurexins, are generated by RGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Sajgo et al., 2017; Shigeoka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to Sajgo et al., 2017; Shigeoka et al., 2016

claim: LRRTM1-neurexin interactions are critical for the formation of complex RG synapses.
source: Therefore, based on our results, we hypothesized that LRRTM1-neurexin interactions are critical for the formation of complex RG synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LRRTM1 is expressed by relay cells, neurexins by RGCs, and loss of LRRTM1 leads to loss of complex RG synapses

claim: The loss of CASK leads to abnormal retinogeniculate connectivity and optic nerve hypoplasia.
source: Although the necessity of neurexins in retinogeniculate connectivity has yet to be thoroughly examined, the loss of CASK, a MAGUK protein necessary for trafficking neurexins to the presynaptic membrane, leads to abnormal retinogeniculate connectivity and optic nerve hypoplasia (LaConte et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2016; Moog et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to LaConte et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2016; Moog et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2017

claim: Neurexins have other postsynaptic partners expressed in visual thalamus, including neuroligins and other LRRTMs.
source: It is important to point out that neurexins have other postsynaptic partners expressed in visual thalamus, including neuroligins and other LRRTMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–G) (Laurén et al., 2003; Varoqueaux et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-G and citations to Laurén et al., 2003; Varoqueaux et al., 2006

claim: Neuroligins and other LRRTMs are capable of inducing excitatory synaptogenesis elsewhere in the brain or in vitro.

evidence: Supported by citations to Fox and Umemori, 2006; Craig et al., 2006; Ko et al., 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2010

claim: Simple and complex RG synapses may be assembled through different postsynaptic interactions with neurexins.
source: The presence of LRRTM1, other LRRTMs, and neuroligins in dLGN raises an interesting possibility that simple and complex RG synapses may be assembled through different postsynaptic interactions with neurexins.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the presence of multiple neurexin-binding partners in dLGN

claim: Relay cells receive a very small number of strong, functional inputs from the retina.
source: It is easy to discount the importance of retinal convergence onto relay cells and the role that complex RG synapses may play in vision, since many groups (including our own [Hammer et al., 2014]) have demonstrated that relay cells receive a very small number of strong, functional inputs from the retina (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005; Hooks and Chen, 2006; Litvina and Chen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammer et al., 2014; Chen and Regehr, 2000; Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005; Hooks and Chen, 2006; Litvina and Chen, 2017

evidence: Supported by citation to Litvina and Chen, 2017

claim: Complex RG synapses are not functionally insignificant artifacts of impaired or incomplete activity-dependent refinement.
source: For these reasons, we believe that results presented here provide the first clues that complex RG synapses (and retinal convergence) are not functionally insignificant artifacts of impaired or incomplete activity-dependent refinement, but rather are an important component of processing and relaying visual information from the retina to visual cortex.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of complex RG synapses leads to specific visual behavioral deficits
